stats.dataNote: Long-distance walkers, pilgrims who walked more than two days, registered on arrival at Nidaros Pilegrimsgård in Trondheim, across all the St. Olav Ways, from the national pilgrim office's 2024 statistics report. Not every pilgrim who reaches the cathedral calls at the reception, so the true number is somewhat higher, and the report counts short walkers separately and only in some years. Its news page gives 1,793 pilgrims received in 2025, 13% more than the year before, without saying whether short walkers are included, so that figure is not in the series. Reused with the office's permission, under ODbL with attribution.

latest.note: Long-distance walkers registered at Nidaros Pilegrimsgård, all routes.

description.en: The inland pilgrim way from Oslo to Nidaros Cathedral in Trondheim: 643 km from the ruins of St Mary's Church in Oslo's medieval town, over Hadeland, past Gjøvik and Lillehammer, through Gudbrandsdalen and across Dovrefjell, then down through Oppdal and Skaun to the cathedral where St Olav is buried. 24 days here, the high point 1,310 m on Dovrefjell, with about 11,960 m of ascent against 11,880 m of descent.

distanceNote.en: 643 km is the rounded sum of the 24 stages, as every linear route here declares, and each stage's figure is the length of route.main.geojson between its own two anchors. That line is the shortest connected path through the eight pinned OpenStreetMap relations, held to the route by every stage anchor in turn, and measured with the repository's own way graph. No published figure set it. It agrees with the 643 km the national pilgrim office gives for the route, a check only (see provenance). Between Oslo and Lillehammer the office's route has two branches, one either side of Lake Mjøsa and of about equal length; this section follows the western one, over Hadeland and through Gjøvik, which is the one relation 1370273 carries. The eastern branch, by Eidsvoll and Hamar, is OpenStreetMap relation 1200009 (Romeriksleden) and is left for a later variant.

estimatedDays.note: typical is the stage count: each stage is one day by construction of the day rule recorded in provenance. min and max are the walked line's 643.0 km at the two ends of that rule's 20-30 km band, rounded up. No published walking time set any of the three. The national pilgrim office gives 32 days for the whole route at about 20 km a day, inside this range; it is a check, not a source.

hoursNote.en: Every stage's estimatedHours is Naismith's rule read at two paces and rounded to whole hours, the rule the four Shikoku dōjō use: min at five kilometres an hour plus 600 m of ascent an hour, max at 3.5 km/h plus 500 m. No roughness factor is applied, because this repository holds no walking times for this route to fit one against, and borrowing Kumano's would assert that a Gudbrandsdalen farm-track day walks like a Kii mountain day. Nothing published was used to check the result either. Read each band as what a day's distance and climbing cost, not as a promise; the 4 days over 34 km carry warnings in stages.json saying why they are that long.

elevationRange.elevationNote: Ascent, descent and every per-stage high and low point are sampled from EU-DEM v1.1, the Copernicus 25 m digital elevation model, at each of the walked line's 31,116 vertices, with a 20 m hysteresis threshold so the model's own noise is not counted as climbing, then rounded to the nearest 10 m — scripts/elevation.ts, applied by npm run apply-elevation, the method kumano-kodo-kohechi was measured with, on a different model. Not SRTM 30 m, the corpus's model, because SRTM stops at 60° N and this route runs from 59.9° to 63.4° N: sampled first, on a planning version of this line, SRTM returned voids for 28,680 of its 31,108 vertices. EU-DEM was built from SRTM and ASTER and covers Scandinavia north of 60°, with a stated vertical accuracy of ±7 m RMSE, inside the 20 m threshold; its figures are therefore close kin to the corpus's SRTM ones but not identical, and are not to be compared with them metre for metre. The totals are the sum of the 24 stages. The high point, 1,310 m, falls on stage 16 (Hjerkinn fjellstue to Ryphusan, 34.2 km).

overview.difficultyNote: moderate is the maintainer's ruling (2026-10-26), not a grading or a measurement: the schema requires an overview difficulty, and no open or official source grades this route. CLAUDE.md's rule — no difficulty written for a route whose stages were measured rather than graded — is kept at stage level, where no stage carries one, as on the four Shikoku dōjō.

terrainNote.en: From OpenStreetMap's tags on the ways the walked line follows, measured segment by segment: 140.9 km paved, 77.0 km gravel or compacted, 20.5 km earth or grass, and 404.9 km with no surface recorded, so terrainTypes says what is tagged and nothing about the untagged majority. 277.7 km is path, track, footway or cycleway and 365.5 km is road. mountain is added for the stages whose measured high point reaches 1,000 m, the crossing of Dovrefjell. Each stage's terrainNotes gives its own figures.

origin.en: The route leads to the grave of Olav II Haraldsson, King of Norway from 1015 to 1028, who died at Stiklestad on 29 July 1030 and is buried in Nidaros Cathedral. He is venerated as a saint, and 29 July, the day of his death, is his feast, Olsok.

description.en: Pilgrims can carry a pilgrim passport (pilegrimspass) and collect stamps in it along the way, at pilgrim hostels, regional pilgrim centres and churches; where a place to stay has no stamp, the host can sign it instead. Carrying one is optional. The passport costs NOK 50 and is sold at the regional pilgrim centres and at other places along the route, among them the centres in Oslo, Granavollen and on Dovrefjell.

minimumDistanceNote.en: The Olavsbrev is given to pilgrims who show a stamped passport for at least the last 100 km on foot to Nidaros Cathedral, or the last 200 km by bicycle. On this route the office suggests Berkåk to Trondheim as a walk that qualifies. Pilgrims who do not qualify can receive a pilgrim diploma instead.

name.en: The pilgrim reception (pilegrimsmottaket) near Nidaros Cathedral, Trondheim

description.en: The feast of St Olav, on the anniversary of his death at Stiklestad in 1030.
Collecting stamps along the way records where a pilgrim has been, and the stamped passport is what the Olavsbrev is given against.
Outside the west front of Nidaros Cathedral stands the last milestone of the route, carrying the pilgrim mark and an inscription saying that no kilometres remain.
Springs associated with St Olav lie at many places along the route; their water was said to heal.
Pilgrims who reach the cathedral are invited to the pilgrim reception nearby, where the last stamps are given, arrivals are counted, and the Olavsbrev is issued to those who qualify.

etiquette.en: Two stretches over Dovrefjell run through calving grounds of wild reindeer. The office asks pilgrims to take care around them, and not to cross before the calving is over, in mid-June.
Where a place to stay has no stamp, ask the host to sign the pilgrim passport instead.

historicalSignificance.en: In the Middle Ages the Gudbrandsdalsleden was the main road to Trondheim and Nidaros Cathedral, where St Olav is buried. Norwegian authorities began restoring the old pilgrim routes in the 1990s, and the St. Olav Ways now total more than 3,800 km, of which about 2,770 km are on land; several of them belong to the association that holds their status as a Council of Europe Cultural Route. The year 2030 marks 1,000 years since St Olav's death at Stiklestad.

accommodationNotes.en: accommodationTypes lists the kinds of lodging OpenStreetMap records within 300 m of the walked line (7 guesthouse, 2 hostel, 13 hotel), and nothing more: it says what is mapped, not what is open, and it is the same coverage the day rule had to work with. Where it runs thin the days run long — stage 4 (Granavollen to Alstad, 49.6 km) is the longest, and stage 21 (Løkken Verk to Hongslo, 8.9 km) the shortest, for the same reason. Across all the St. Olav Ways the office counts more than 500 places to stay, from pilgrim hostels, many of them on farms, to cabins, campsites and hotels.

emergencyNote.en: Wikidata (Q20, P2852) lists 112, 113 and 110 as Norway's emergency numbers.

notes.en: The national pilgrim office recommends walking between 1 June and 1 September, to avoid snow and meltwater; places to stay may be closed outside that window. Do not cross Dovrefjell before about 10 June: until then the crossing has no infrastructure in place, the bridges over the Hondyrju and Vesle Hondyrju rivers are laid out only around that date, snow can hide the waymarks, and wild reindeer are calving. Even in summer the temperature on the plateau can fall towards 0 °C, and the office suggests taking the train over Dovre when the crossing is not open.

transportNotes.en: transportLinks lists, for each stage boundary, the nearest railway station within 3 km that lies beside the national network (within 150 m of a railway=rail line tagged usage=main or branch), and the airport at each end, all from OpenStreetMap. The national pilgrim office notes that trains run alongside almost the whole route.

sources.notes: Eight relations of the Pilegrimsleden superroute 1370274 — the osm block below says which and how each was confirmed. Read through the Overpass instance at maps.mail.ru and the OpenStreetMap API, because overpass-api.de refused connections from the environment this section was built in; the database and its licence are the same. Every stage anchor is an OpenStreetMap node or way, recorded in that anchor's own note in stages.json. The service waypoints are enrich-waypoints' own POI query, run in 120 tiles along route.geojson rather than as one box from Oslo to Trondheim, which the mirror would not answer; 90 of the tiles came from the OpenStreetMap API's map call, filtered to that query's exact tags, when the mirror kept timing out. A node within 300 m of route.geojson lies inside some tile, so the waypoints are the ones the single query would have kept. The curated waypoints are the churches and sites the drafted stage text names, each carrying its OpenStreetMap id in osmId.

sources.name: Derived from the walked line
sources.notes: The day divisions are cut by rule rather than taken from a guidebook, so they can be re-run; no guidebook or official stage list was used, because the national pilgrim office's site states no licence. The rule ends each day where OpenStreetMap shows a bed. A candidate is either a named lodging — tourism hostel, guest_house, hotel, motel, alpine_hut, wilderness_hut, camp_site or chalet — within 500 m of the walked line, or a named settlement — place city, town, village, hamlet or suburb — within 500 m of the line with a named lodging within 1.5 km of it and of the line. A lodging candidate is anchored on the nearest named settlement within 1.5 km of it and 500 m of the line where there is one, and on the lodging itself where there is not, so a day is named for the place a walker would say they reached. Named means a non-empty name. 500 m is the radius build-ways snaps a stage boundary across. From each day's start, the day ends at the candidate nearest 25 km ahead among those 20 to 30 km ahead, the earlier of two equally near; where that band is empty it ends at the candidate nearest 25 km among all those strictly ahead, which is what keeps the cut advancing through stretches with no mapped lodging. Once the cathedral is no more than 30 km ahead, the day ends there. Position along the line is the perpendicular projection onto route.main.geojson, in a local plane per segment, with distance along the line summed by haversine. Each stage's distanceKm is the length of route.main.geojson between its own two anchors as build-ways cuts it, rounded to one decimal, and each anchor's note says which arm chose it and for which lodging. Every waypoint's stageIndex and kmFromStart is derived from the same line and the same cut: a waypoint belongs to the stage whose stretch of route.main.geojson holds the perpendicular projection of its coordinate, and kmFromStart is where that projection falls, in km from the section's start, rounded to one decimal.

The two-branch fact in distanceNote is also theirs.

osm.note: The Gudbrandsdalsleden has no Wikidata item, so there was no P402 to follow; the relations were found by tag search and confirmed by their own tags. All eight are members of superroute 1370274 (name=Pilegrimsleden, website=https://pilegrimsleden.no/, pilgrimage=yes), and they chain end to end, south to north. 1370273 is name=Gudbrandsdalsleden, website=https://pilegrimsleden.no/no/map/gudbrandsdalsleden, description:no naming the way from Oslo over Hadeland and through Gudbrandsdalen towards Nidaros, covering Oslo to Lillehammer. 5659125 is name=Gudbrandsdalsleden (Lillehammer-Dovre). 3917970, 3918309 and 1671572 are name=Kongeveien over Dovre with ref=DOV61, DOV62 and DOV63 and from/to tags running Dovre-Fokstugu, Fokstugu-Hageseter, Hageseter-Kongsvold; 5677571 is Kongeveien over Dovre (Kongsvoll-Oppdal) and 5697677 Kongeveien over Dovre (Oppdal-Skaun). All five carry wikidata=Q11995693, which Wikidata labels Pilegrimsleia over Dovrefjell — the pilgrim way over Dovrefjell — which is what makes them this route and not only the old King's Road. 5659103 is name=Gudbrandsdalsleden (Skaun-Nidaros), with the same website and description as 1370273, and ends at Nidaros Cathedral. Order matters: geometry.ts concatenates in this order. Variants are left out: the superroute's other members are other St. Olav ways, for later sections, and the spurs inside these eight are what build-main-line's shortest path leaves behind. As first fetched on 2026-10-26 the eight did not form one connected line: six breaks, five where an existing way joining two members was not itself a member, and one where a member road stopped 3.6 m short of the track it continues along. They were fixed upstream the same day, not spliced here: changesets 191073648, 191073650, 191073653 and 191073659 add the five ways (splitting Konventveien in Oslo so only its 3.2 m connecting piece joins 1370273), and changeset 191073959 joins the road to the track, whose 81 m between the two members it now links joins 5697677. OpenStreetMap note 5601886 described that last gap before it was mapped. The walked line is the relations' own geometry, with no join of this repository's.
